Nov 3 : Supercomputer maker Bull and Schwarz Digits, the technology arm of Lidl-owner Schwarz Group, signed a preliminary agreement on Tuesday to jointly develop AI computing services that would operate entirely under European jurisdiction, a link-up of two companies with big AI bets. Under the agreement, Schwarz Digits will offer the service through its STACKIT business, which rents out computing power and data storage over the internet. Bull, the state-owned French maker of Europe's fastest supercomputers, will handle manufacturing. The two companies plan to design servers filling the data centres together, and could eventually offer business software from Germany’s SAP through the partnership, they said. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Companies and public bodies using STACKIT will also be able to use Bull’s software for building and running AI applications directly on the service.

Nov 3 : Apple shares tumbled about 4 per cent on Tuesday as its first results under new CEO John Ternus showed that rising memory chip costs were denting the iPhone maker's envied margins, the latest sign of the AI boom's toll on the technology industry. Sales of smartphones, PCs and other electronics have already suffered this year from price hikes driven by soaring memory chip costs as the AI industry's data-center race absorbs supply. That even Apple, long known for its supply-chain prowess, is feeling the squeeze shows virtually no firm is spared. The warning follows Intel's bleak forecast last week on collapsing PC chip demand. "What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.

"For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Gross margin, the share of revenue Apple keeps after production costs, slipped to 47.9 per cent in the September quarter from the June quarter, even with the boost from tariff refunds. The company expects its gross margin to shrink further to between 45 per cent and 46 per cent in the December quarter, as it also grapples with the costs of rolling out an AI-powered Siri that is central to its AI plans. To cushion the blow, Apple has been drawing on memory chips bought earlier at lower prices and has moved to lock in supplies. Its manufacturing purchase obligations, or orders placed with suppliers and contract manufacturers, increased by $33 billion to $89.7 billion as of Sept. 26, a filing showed. TERNUS' PRODUCT BLITZ Apple's drop on Tuesday also weighed on the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. Expectations were high going into the results because Apple's restraint on AI spending had made it a refuge for investors uneasy about the AI boom's soaring costs, helping its shares gain by more than a fifth so far this year. The memory crunch comes just as Ternus rolls out a product blitz packed with Apple firsts, including its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo, and its first touchscreen MacBooks. Apple has also been raising prices to cushion the hit to profitability. That, along with strong demand for the premium iPhone 18 Pro lineup, helped it beat fourth-quarter sales estimates and forecast upbeat revenue. But some analysts warn that more price hikes risk scaring off buyers as inflation is already climbing. The CEO comments imply "Apple products are going to become even more expensive, which is not ideal at a time when the consumer is feeling the pinch from a higher cost of living," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. Apple is set to lose over $170 billion in market value from its $4.94 trillion valuation, if losses hold. The stock trades at nearly 35 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, compared with 18.23 times for Alphabet and 23.43 times for Microsoft.

Nov 3 : Elon Musk’s recent super-sized pay packages at SpaceX and Tesla were centered on some eye-popping goals: creating a 1 million-person human colony on Mars, putting a million robotaxis on the road and selling a million humanoid robots. A merger combining Musk’s trillion-dollar rocket and electric vehicle firms would mean he might not ever need to meet those lofty targets to achieve his ultimate goal: control over his corporate empire. Musk said on a SpaceX earnings call last month that both companies' boards had formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. A deal could give him the voting control at Tesla that he has said he wants, without his having to hit any of the milestones in his pay plan. As for Musk’s compensation, a merger initially would likely award him only a sliver of the $1 trillion in stock from last year’s widely discussed Tesla pay package, according to a Reuters review of the plan and six executive-compensation experts. SpaceX’s board could also restructure his compensation plan after a potential Tesla deal, the experts said.

An examination of Musk’s compensation packages at both companies shows that the structure of SpaceX’s plan, which gives Musk voting power upfront before earning the stock, helps provide a shortcut to gaining control of Tesla. That makes the provocative, futuristic Mars and humanoid robot goals more of an afterthought, according to the experts who reviewed the plans for Reuters. “It’s irrelevant,” said Charles Elson, founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware. “This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control.” 'AMBITIOUS STUFF' The $1 trillion Tesla compensation plan that shareholders approved for Musk last year required him to hit a series of market-capitalization and operational milestones in order to collect more stock and amass more voting control. Leading up to SpaceX’s IPO this summer, the company’s board granted Musk stock awards tied to boosting the company’s market cap, getting a million people to Mars and building massive space data centers. Unless Musk achieved the Mars and data center goals, he could not pocket the shares, according to the agreements. Importantly, though, Musk immediately got all the voting power associated with those shares, just not the economic rights. That got him to 85 per cent control over SpaceX without needing to hit any goals. Musk already had significant ownership in SpaceX before being awarded those additional voting rights. Matthew Bloomfield, an associate professor of accounting at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said he viewed the SpaceX plan, crafted so close to the IPO, as “just a marketing document.” “You put a bunch of ambitious stuff in there and a lot of people say, ‘Look at this big bet Elon Musk is putting on himself,’” he said. In reality, the plan is mostly about “getting a bunch of people hyped,” he said. Musk, Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The story at Tesla is the opposite. A flashy compensation package that awarded Musk up to $1 trillion in Tesla stock last year was designed to give him more control over the company, but only as he meets operational and market-cap goals over time. Musk has not yet achieved any of the targets in the Tesla plan. Even if he were to hit all of the goals, including increasing the company's market cap nearly eightfold, he would have only about 29 per cent of the voting power at Tesla, according to documents the board presented last year. As Tesla’s board was shopping the plan to investors last year, Musk himself said that gaining more control over Tesla was the goal, highlighting the risks of building AI-powered robots. “My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ousted at some point in the future?” he said on an October 2025 Tesla earnings call. MERGER OFFERS SHORTCUT TO TESLA CONTROL A merger offers a far quicker path to getting that control. Barclays analysts estimated in a recent investor note that at the current size of each company, if SpaceX were to acquire Tesla, then Musk would own about 37 per cent of the new conglomerate but have 56 per cent of the voting power. That is because many of his SpaceX shares are in a special class that carries 10 times the voting rights of the typical shareholder. There is no such class of shares at Tesla. Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla compensation plans contemplate what would happen in the event of a merger. For Tesla, the language in the agreement is straightforward. In a “change in control” event such as an acquisition by SpaceX, Musk could receive stock payouts for meeting market-cap goals without the added requirement of an operational goal like having 1 million robotaxis in operation. The market cap would be calculated based on the stock price immediately before the merger or the value that Tesla shareholders receive from the transaction, whichever is greater. Tesla’s current market capitalization is about $1.6 trillion. That would need to grow to $2 trillion in connection with the merger for Musk to receive any stock awards under the plan. (Meeting that goal would issue him $20 billion in Tesla shares at a $2 trillion valuation, though it would be worth less because the plan only compensates Musk for stock growth after his pay plan was announced, in September 2025.) Musk could receive more if the market capitalization grew to $2.5 trillion, $3 trillion or higher after a deal, though the six compensation experts said such a premium would be unlikely. SPACEX BOARD COULD REVISE MUSK'S PLAN The SpaceX compensation plan is less specific about what happens in the event of a merger, and compensation experts said the board could significantly adjust Musk's plan after a transaction. Musk’s plan at SpaceX is divided into two parts: a series of market-cap goals, paired with a goal of setting up a colony on Mars with a million people; and another set of market-cap goals, alongside a target of building space data centers capable of “delivering 100 terawatts of compute per year.” Musk said on X earlier this year that 100 terawatts per year would be "200 times the current electricity output of Earth," and would require manufacturing satellites on the moon that would be "shot into deep space." Musk is already able to vote all the shares awarded to him in the SpaceX plan, but he cannot get any value out of them unless he achieves those goals. So even if he more than triples the value of SpaceX, and gets 500,000 people to Mars, he would not earn any of the shares, according to the plan. The shares in Musk's plan would be worth $719 billion at the highest market cap target, based on SpaceX's current shares outstanding, according to research firm Equilar. Kevin Murphy, a finance professor at USC's Marshall School of Business and an expert witness for Tesla in defending Musk’s 2018 pay package, said he thinks the board and Musk are likely to keep all the plans in place. They could simply increase the market-cap and earnings goals, and adjust the share awards, to account for the larger combined company, he said. SpaceX did something similar earlier this year when it acquired xAI and assumed Musk’s compensation plan from that firm. Though Musk’s SpaceX plan has incredibly difficult goals, four of the compensation experts said the board could likely amend the plan however it wants. With Musk already owning nearly half of SpaceX, whether he ultimately gets a million people to Mars and pockets the additional stock from his compensation plan is less important than the control, the compensation experts said. Murphy acknowledged that goals like the Mars colony are “pretty pie-in-the-sky,” but said Musk is not likely to want an easy payday upfront. “He’s an all-or-nothing kind of guy,” Murphy said. “He doesn't want a couple cookies. He wants the whole bag.”

Source: Reuters

While tech-related borrowing in Europe has lagged the United States, investors say that leaves scope for a larger wave of issuance across euro, sterling and Swiss franc markets in coming months. Alphabet launched its second euro-denominated bond sale this year on Monday, following a €9 billion ($10 billion) issue in May. Investors expect other so-called hyperscalers — or Big Tech companies — including Meta, Amazon and Microsoft, to increase borrowing outside the US as they fund large-scale AI infrastructure investments.

"Europe has been behind the US in terms of issuance in the tech space but the activity is accelerating," said Marion Le Morhedec, chief investment officer for fixed income at Fidelity International. She estimates that €40 billion to €60 billion of issuance is in the pipeline. Issuing debt in foreign currencies also allows companies to hedge the currency risk from their global assets, while taking advantage of relatively lower borrowing costs in markets like Europe. Europe's deep capital markets offer an attractive source of funding. But while greater issuance expands the pool of highly rated corporate debt available to investors, it could also raise borrowing costs for European companies and governments already grappling with fiscal and inflation concerns. TECH BORROWING ACCELERATES IN EUROPE US markets have absorbed more than $250 billion of technology-related debt issuance so far this year, up 81 per cent from the same period last year. In Europe, issuance totals $39.3 billion, up about 5 per cent year-on-year, LSEG data shows. Despite investor concerns over whether Big Tech's massive AI investments will deliver returns quickly enough — spurring a selloff which erased more than $2 trillion from the tech-heavy Nasdaq's market value last month — analysts and investors expect bond issuance to remain strong. BNP Paribas expects euro-denominated investment-grade corporate bond net supply to rise 83 per cent to €192 billion ($214 billion) in 2027, up from €105 billion this year. Offshore bond issuance by US companies — dubbed the "reverse Yankee" in reference to Yankee bonds — is forecast to account for around €80 billion to €90 billion of the 2027 total debt supply, with hyperscalers making up the bulk of that, said Giulio Baratta, global co-head of investment grade finance at BNP Paribas. "It is undeniable that if any of these hyperscalers go into the market with a multi-billion deal to execute in a day, everybody knows about it and everybody needs to pay attention," said Baratta, who helped arrange Alphabet's May euro bond sale. JUMBO DEALS COULD TEST DEMAND The influx of debt could widen investment-grade credit spreads as hyperscalers compete with other highly rated borrowers across sectors such as utilities, telecommunications and automakers for investor demand. Asset swap spreads on the ICE BofA Euro Investment Grade index widened by 11 basis points last month, suggesting investors are demanding greater compensation to hold corporate bonds relative to interest-rate swaps. Issuers may need to offer pricing concessions to secure sufficient demand as supply expands, analysts say, potentially raising funding costs for other companies. Investors in European markets also have less experience absorbing the multitranche transactions that have become commonplace in the US. Such deals could therefore temporarily widen European investment-grade credit spreads, said Jonathan Owen, a member of TwentyFour Asset Management's multi-sector bond portfolio management team. SOME EUROPEAN ISSUERS SHIFT TO SHORTER MATURITIES Strong investor demand has so far absorbed the supply. But a series of jumbo deals of €10 billion to €20 billion could test that appetite, particularly if several issuers come to market simultaneously, analysts said. Some European companies are already responding to volatile long-term yields and expectations of heavier issuance by favouring shorter maturities, investors say. "We definitely observe that corporate, non-hyperscaler corporate issuers are staying away from the long end," said Vontobel portfolio manager Christian Hantel, without naming specific companies. "What has been a normal 10-year maturity bond, now they move to five to seven years." The additional issuance could further weigh on government bond markets, which are already under pressure from investor worries about fiscal and inflation risks. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said last week that debt issuance by hyperscalers had contributed to rising sovereign bond yields. "People are very much focused on the amount of AI supply that we're getting at the long end and what that means for government bonds," Owen said, adding that hyperscaler debt offers high credit quality while typically yielding more than government bonds. HONG KONG, Nov 3 : Tech companies will need to raise more capital to help meet the enormous demand for the AI industry's growth boom, but there is a risk of an industry correction, global financial leaders said on Tuesday. Tech stocks globally have faced pressure in recent weeks as growing concerns about AI spending trigger a new wave of selloffs, with combined spending set to exceed $730 billion this year, up from about $700 billion. Most of the major tech companies were expected to raise more capital to keep up with the enormous likely demand from the AI industry's growth, said Jon Gray, president of Blackstone, which is an active investor in AI infrastructure. "Now you're in an environment where the demand's running well ahead of supply," Gray said at an investment gathering in Hong Kong, citing "pretty extraordinary" demand for computing power.

"So that gives me a lot of comfort," he added. "Meta and Google and Oracle raising equity ... SpaceX going public, Anthropic going public," Gray said. "On top of it ... the data centers, the energy needs are enormous." STRONG COMPANIES WITH 'GOOD STORIES' Despite some AI-related market upheavals, strong companies with "good stories" would still be able to raise capital, though the industry's strong growth could create volatility for investors, said Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon. "But things will go wrong too, and we'll get things wrong," he added at the event, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit. "Investors will find situations where they pick wrong, where they lose money ... It's important to have a balanced, diversified view." JPMorgan Vice Chairman Daniel Pinto said he was bullish on AI, but the market was pricing in revenue and earnings growth for related companies that was too steep. "I do believe that it has a positive, slow curve and it may not be as steep as the market is pricing," he said. "So I think that it could be a correction in the AI sector," he said, adding that other firms with high valuations related to AI could come under pressure as the industry started to recalibrate its expectations. Last month, S&P said it expected the top six US hyperscalers - Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta and SpaceX - to spend more than $7 trillion on data centers and other AI-related capex between 2025 and 2030, while having negative free cash flow until at least next year. Citadel Securities Chief Executive Peng Zhao said the sheer scale of capital and growth in AI was proving difficult for some investors to value correctly, which was adding to volatility in the sector. "Our ability to really know what this technology will do and its revenue potential is very, very limited due to the fact that we've never seen anything like this," he said. "It's not so much that people all of a sudden develop a bearish view of what the technology can accomplish, but it's rather the sudden realization that we can only know so much ... the numbers involved are so huge." Morgan Stanley Chief Executive Ted Pick flagged emerging early signs of US markets edging close to a correction, with a majority of stocks in major indices off nearly 10 per cent. The latest test of investor appetite is a sale of €6 billion ($6.7 billion) in bonds on Monday by Google parent Alphabet. ASIA-PAC TECH FUNDRAISING MORE THAN TRIPLED Fundraising by Asia-Pacific tech companies more than tripled to $125.8 billion in the first three quarters of 2026 from $36 billion a year earlier. The growth was driven by a wave of semiconductor and AI-related deals, such as Chinese chipmaker CXMT’s $9.8-billion IPO and Enflame Technology's $910.6-million listing, LSEG data shows. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta have signalled that spending on AI will not slow. In one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout, Blackstone agreed last week to provide financing of $63 billion with Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic. The rising cost of capital and some of today's scepticism will slow the pace, however, Gray added. "But the overall trend is towards greater investment and therefore more needs for multiple forms of capital." Emmanuel Roman, CEO of asset manager PIMCO, said AI financing deals are attractive, with more coming for the firm.

SYDNEY, Nov 3 : Australia's largest pension fund, the A$430 billion ($301.7 billion) AustralianSuper, said it will stick to the "picks and shovels" of the AI industry as it navigates unprecedented turbulence in the market for global tech stocks.  Mark Hargraves, the head of AustralianSuper's international equities and private equity business, said the fund believed chipmakers and hyperscaler data centres would weather the current storm engulfing the AI sector. The comments show how one of Australia's biggest investors is positioning its AI holdings as doubts grow over whether the sector's earnings can justify its astronomical valuations.  One of the Melbourne-based firm's largest AI-linked exposures in its balanced portfolio is Nvidia, where it holds about A$3.05 billion worth of stock, according to recent filings. It holds more of the chipmaker's stock in other fund options.

AustralianSuper also owns about A$2.3 billion each in Microsoft and Alphabet, the filings show, as well as stakes in SK Hynix, SpaceX, Meta, Broadcom and Micron. "Large language models require compute power and the hyperscalers are providing that with the data centres, and that compute is driven by chips," Hargraves told Reuters in an interview on October 28.  "We've been quite focused on what we call the picks and shovels. But as the landscape is evolving, then we ... see the opportunity sets developing and we kind of move exposures accordingly." Globally, AI shares have stumbled amid growing doubts over whether earnings can keep pace with lofty valuations, prompting investors to reassess crowded positions after a prolonged rally. Still, many fund managers remain bullish on the sector's long-term prospects, betting demand for AI chips, data centres and related infrastructure has further to run. AI and AI-related stocks now made up about 40 per cent of the global equities market, Hargraves said, adding that the growth of the industry and its influence on markets had been the fastest emergence of a major investment theme he had seen in more than 30 years working in equities. "I've seen a lot of evolution over time. I think this cycle, the rate of evolution is happening faster than previous cycles," he said. "Some of the volatility you're seeing is reflective of that speed of change. It is leading things to change quite quickly and the best is having to constantly reassess things." Hargraves said that while AustralianSuper was a pre-IPO investor in Anthropic, he would not comment on the fund's intention in the upcoming share sale that would value the US company at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Instead, he said the IPO would give investors a greater insight into the financial forecasts of the large language models. ($1 = 1.4253 Australian dollars)

HONG KONG, Nov 3 : The dollar wavered alongside oil prices on Tuesday on hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran, while the Aussie was steady ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia's rate decision. Brent crude futures plunged more than 7 per cent on Monday in their sharpest single-day drop in months, after Tehran said its contacts with the US aimed at ending their eight-month war were continuing. Falling energy prices helped ease inflation concerns and dragged longer-dated US Treasury yields lower. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was steady at 4.9145 per cent, while that on the 30-year bond was also flat at 5.2868 per cent. Both had dipped to their lowest levels in nearly two months in the previous session.

The dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, last traded a shade weaker at 101.76 after dropping to a one-month low on Monday. Meanwhile, an AI-driven stock market slump showed little sign of slowing down, hurting risk sentiment and lending some support to the dollar. Tensions around US midterm elections also loom large, helping to prop up the dollar as a safe-haven play. "Oil relief is growing, but conviction elsewhere remains thin," Sim Moh Siong, FX strategist at OCBC, said in a note. "Cheaper energy is reshaping FX dynamics, while AI concerns and US election risks reinforce our view that the USD remains supported." The euro was a touch higher at $1.1185 on the back of dollar weakness. The Japanese yen was flat at 157.915 per dollar during a local holiday. ANOTHER ROUND OF CENTRAL BANK MEETINGS Multiple central banks are scheduled to issue policy statements this week, including those in Britain, Australia, Norway and Sweden. The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent on Tuesday, which would be the highest level since December 2008. The move would bring total tightening this year across five increases to 125 basis points. The Australian dollar was little changed at $0.7002. The kiwi was flat at $0.5617. Sterling strengthened 0.05 per cent to $1.3414 after PMI data showed British manufacturers started the final quarter of 2026 with the strongest output growth in more than two years. Economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of England to raise its Bank Rate to 4.0 per cent from 3.75 per cent, the first hike since August 2023, when inflation was still more than triple its 2 per cent target.
